item.content:encoded:
The material has been found to reflect all radiation with 100% efficiency.

This would make great radiation shielding. A metal structure resembling double paned glass, with a hollow space in the middle, filled with this. Provided it weren't damaged, this could contain a nuclear meltdown. Plus, if the inside were damaged, say by a meltdown, SCP-357 would expand to cover the reactor.

This would work great for the Foundation's reactors. (I assume an organisation as energy-hungry as the Foundation uses nuclear reactors for power.)

My point is that saying "radiation" is pretty pointless, but it wasn't listed as "energy" which would just have me frothing at the mouth. The description given makes this stuff the perfect mirror, by the way. It would appear silver.

And I really did mean thermal radiation: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiation#Thermal_radiation_.28heat.29

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: You make good points, save for the bit about reflecting thermal energy. Energy. If you meant infrared, then yes I'd assume it would be reflected, but thermal energy is not necessarily imparted by radiation. There's three methods of heat transfer as I recall; conduction, convection, and radiation. It could be heated through conduction, which would essentially just be touching it with hot stuff. In the case described here, 'hot stuff' would be heated air molecules.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
If allowed to settle on a flat surface, SCP-357 will spread until its average thickness is no more than 1 mm.

You mean no LESS than 1 mm. Or "…is approximately 1 mm."

The material has been found to reflect all radiation with 100% efficiency.

Sooo… thermal? How do you heat it up? Maybe "Electromagnetic radiation"?

If solid matter is placed in a container of SCP-357, it will sink into the substance at a constant rate of 0.5 cm per minute.

I can't tell if they meant that things with a lighter density don't "float" on it, which would be VERY odd.

If a homogeneous pressure of at least 100 N/cm2 is applied to a sample of SCP-357, the material will decrease in size at a rate of 1.3 cm3 per minute or more, depending on the magnitude of the pressure.

I… wait. If you put it in a pressurized container is disappearance is LINEAR?! Misread this. Still, damned odd. Not sure if decrease in size (volume) implied a decrease in mass.

Details: A pressure of 100 N/cm2 is applied to SCP-357. The sample is able to be compressed to only 0.01 mm3. While still compressed, the sample is allowed to return to room temperature. When pressure is removed, the sample immediately returns to a volume of 1 mm3.

I don't think that's consistent with the implied effect of the above test. It LOOKED like it would just decrease the volume. Period. As it is, this is indestructible gray goo and will eventually eat the planet.
